text.0_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: The word of Hashem: In the first two chapters, he prophesies about the locust swarm that came in those days and devastated the land:
text.0_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: Hear this, O elders: He addresses: 1) the elders, who should recall whether anything like this had occurred in previous generations; 2) give ear, all inhabitants of the land, who should recount this extraordinary event to their children after them. Corresponding to “Hear this, O elders,” he explains: Has this happened in your days, even though you have already lived many years? And corresponding to “Give ear, all inhabitants of the land,” he says:
text.0_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Tell your children about it: All the inhabitants of the land should recount this event and transmit it as a tradition to future generations, namely:
text.0_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust devoured: Although there was also a devastating locust plague in Egypt, concerning which it is said that nothing like it would occur afterward, only one kind of locust appeared there, whereas here there were four kinds. Each one destroyed whatever its predecessor had left behind. Such a thing had never happened before, as our Sages explained:
text.0_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Awaken: (This entire passage continues through verse 8, where he poetically depicts the vine lamenting, as will be explained there. It is as though the vine wails, takes up a lament, and says:) You drunkards, who are perpetually sunk in the stupor of drunkenness, now awaken from your wine-induced stupor and weep, for there is no intoxicating feast. Moreover, wail, all you wine drinkers: even those who are not drunkards but are merely accustomed to drinking wine should also wail over the sweet wine, for it has been cut off from your mouths, and you no longer have the pleasant drink that delights your palate.
text.0_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: For a nation has invaded My land: He portrays the locusts as a nation because they are united together like a distinct people. It is mighty in the quality of its strength and without number in its vast multitude. Its teeth—the lion’s strength lies in its teeth, while the strength of the young lion lies in its jaws; thus, it has the teeth of a lion and the jaws of a young lion with which to destroy everything.
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: He has laid My vine waste: For it destroyed the vine and the fig tree by stripping them bare, removing the bark from the trees.
text.0_Chapter, 6_Verse, 1_Comment: And cast it away: It cast away the bark of the trees, until their branches turned white; as a result, the trees were destroyed.
text.0_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Lament like a virgin: In his figurative language, the prophet portrays the vine and the fig tree themselves as wailing the words spoken in verses 5–7. The vine tells the drunkards to weep because a nation has invaded the vine’s land and laid its vine waste. All this is spoken by the vine and the fig tree that were destroyed. He depicts them as a virgin clothed in sackcloth for the husband of her youth. This is an exceptionally striking poetic image. The locusts devoured and destroyed the branches of the vine and the fig tree, leaving only their trunks. It is customary to wrap sackcloth around a trunk from which the bark has been removed, to bind and warm it so that it will grow new shoots and branches. This is the image of being “clothed in sackcloth.” In the terminology of the Sages, a tree that has never been cut down is called a “virgin,” as stated in the first chapter of Niddah: “There are three virgins,” one of which is “a virgin sycamore”—a sycamore that has never been cut down. Accordingly, he portrays the vine, which had never previously been cut down, as a virgin, for until now it had remained untouched. He calls the branches that were cut from it its “husband,” because they rise above it. This virgin now wears sackcloth in mourning for her husband, who has been cut down and taken from her. She is commanded to utter the lament stated above: “For a nation has invaded my land”—that is, the soil upon which she grows—and has destroyed its vine and its fig tree.
text.0_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Cut off: Now he describes why the priests, the ministers of Hashem, mourn: they lament because the meal offering and the libation have been cut off from the House of Hashem, since there is no flour for the meal offerings, nor wine or oil for the libations.
text.0_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Devastated: Corresponding to “the meal offering has been cut off,” he explains that the field has been devastated—the grain fields where wheat for the meal offerings grew. Corresponding to “the libation has been cut off,” he explains that the ground mourns, for the vines used to produce the libations grew upon it. Elaborating on “the field has been devastated,” he says, “for the grain has been devastated,” since grain grows in the field. Elaborating on “the ground mourns,” he says, “the new wine has dried up; the oil languishes,” referring to the wine and oil used for the libations. He then explains further:
text.0_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Corresponding to “the grain has been devastated,” he says, “the farmers are ashamed,” for they are the ones who work the grain fields. Corresponding to “the new wine has dried up,” he says, “wail, O vine growers,” for they are the ones who cultivate vineyards of grapes and olives. He then further explains “the farmers are ashamed” by adding, “over the wheat and over the barley,” as well as “for the harvest of the field has perished,” referring to the other kinds of grain and legumes that grow in the field and are cultivated by farmers. Corresponding to “wail, O vine growers,” he explains:
text.0_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: The vine has dried up, and the fig tree languishes: Those who cultivate vineyards also plant all kinds of fruit trees, and all of them were destroyed. Here he enumerates the seven species for which the Land of Israel is praised: wheat, barley, grapevines, figs, pomegranates, dates, and olives—the olive being included among the vineyards, as explained above. Regarding produce of the ground, he adds, “the harvest of the field has perished,” to include every kind. Regarding trees, he adds the apple tree, the most important of the remaining kinds of trees, and includes them all in the words, “all the trees of the field have dried up.” People were accustomed to rejoice with fruit from the trees on joyous occasions. Concerning this, he says, “for joy has withered away from mankind.”
text.0_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Gird yourselves: He commands the priests to gird themselves with sackcloth for prayer and to lament over the calamity. This is addressed to the priests in general. He then explains that he is speaking to two groups among them: one group should gird themselves with sackcloth and pray, while the other should wail and lament like those who despair without hope. There were righteous priests who were ministers of Hashem, serving Hashem with proper intention, while other priests were merely ministers of the altar, performing its sacrifices but not serving Hashem with the desired intention. Therefore, he says, “Wail, O ministers of the altar”: those who merely minister to the altar should wail in despair, for their prayers are not favorably received. “Come, spend the night in sackcloth, O ministers of my God”: the righteous, however, who truly serve Hashem, should spend the night in sackcloth, praying and repenting so as to avert the decree. He explains why the priests, more than the rest of the people, should be stirred to do this: “For the meal offering and the libation have been withheld from the House of your God.” Because of the locusts, the wheat used for the meal offerings had spoiled and become worm-infested, and the wine used for the libations had been ruined.
text.0_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Sanctify a fast: He further commands the priests to sanctify a fast and proclaim a solemn assembly, so that the people will gather at the House of Hashem. They are to assemble the elders and all the inhabitants of the land in the House of Hashem and cry out to Hashem. During fasts held in response to calamities, they would assemble the people and appoint an elder to lead the prayers, and the elder would deliver words intended to humble and inspire them, as explained in Tractate Taanit.
text.0_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Alas: They should cry out and say, “Alas for the day!” for two reasons: 1) because the day is near—the decree will soon come; and 2) because it will come like devastation from the Almighty, from which there is no way to escape. It is as though the devastation comes from Hashem and through His Divine Providence. Although the natural order does not require this devastation, it comes from the Almighty, who overpowers the natural order—and who can withstand the wrath of Hashem?
text.0_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: Is it not before our eyes? The prophet adds that although the event has not yet actually occurred, we already see it with our own eyes—through the prophetic vision that beholds the future as though it were present. It already stands before our eyes: food has been cut off, and joy and gladness have already been cut off from the House of our God, for songs were sung in the Temple when the libations were offered, as explained by Maimonides in the Laws of the Temple Vessels.
text.0_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: They have rotted: The heaps of grain hidden underground in the field, arranged in separate piles, have also spoiled and become moldy beneath the clods of earth, even though the locusts could not reach them there. He adds that the storehouses have become desolate, where grain was stored, and the granaries have also been demolished—these being smaller than the storehouses—because the grain has dried up.
text.0_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: How the animals groan! The prophet asks in astonishment: If man sinned, what sin did the animals commit? Why should the animals groan—what wrong have they done? Why are the herds of cattle bewildered because they have no pasture? Have even the flocks of sheep incurred guilt? Have they too sinned and become culpable? Why, then, has Hashem punished the animals?
text.0_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: To You: He adds: If you answer that the punishment was principally directed against man, and that domesticated animals perished together with him because they are under his authority and constitute his property—for he was sentenced to lose his animals and possessions—the prophet responds: Yet to You, O Hashem, I cry, for fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness, where there is no human settlement, and a flame has scorched all the trees of the field, even though they are far from human habitation. As a result:
text.0_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: Even the beasts of the field cry out to You: Because of this, even the wild animals, which are not under human dominion, cry out in protest, for the channels of water have dried up, and they have no water to drink.
text.0_Chapter, 19_Verse, 1_Comment: And fire has consumed the pastures of the wilderness, leaving them nothing to graze upon. Therefore, concerning this, to You, O Hashem, I cry: What sin did the wild animals commit, and why should they be punished for man’s transgression?
text.1_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: Sound: (Until now, he has spoken of the time when the prophet announced the coming of the locusts, having seen this decree in prophecy. He now begins a second subject, speaking of the time when the locust swarm had already stirred and begun to invade the land.) Sound the shofar, as required when an alarm is raised over calamities. The blast of the shofar served to assemble the people; therefore, he commanded them to sound it in Zion, throughout the city, so that all its inhabitants would hear. The alarm blast served to arouse fear so that the people would repent; therefore, he says, “Sound the alarm on My holy mountain,” meaning in the Temple. Through this, all the inhabitants of the land will tremble and fear Hashem. For the day of Hashem has come, for it is near. Regarding a human being, we cannot say that his decree has arrived until it actually arrives, for as long as it has not yet arrived, distance stands between it and its destination, and it may be delayed and never arrive. With Hashem, however, once the appointed time is near and there is no temporal interval remaining, we may say that it has already arrived, for nothing can obstruct His decree. Therefore, since the time is near, the day of Hashem has already come.
text.1_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: A day of darkness: He portrays the day as one of darkness and gloom because of the absence of light. It is also a day of cloud and thick darkness—not merely darkness caused by the absence of light, but a tangible darkness produced by vapors and dense mists that obscure the light. Through this darkness, the spreading locust swarm appears like the dawn spread over the mountains in the morning: it can be seen upon the mountaintops, gleaming and shining from afar. It is a numerous people in quantity and mighty in strength, the like of which has never been, for it consisted of four species, something that did not occur in Egypt, as explained above.
text.1_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: Before it, fire devours: He depicts how it consumes and destroys every tree and plant like a fire that devours and burns. It is as though, when it approaches, a fire goes before it and consumes everything; and when it departs, nothing remains for the fire to consume, so it resembles a flame that blazes behind the fire, scorching the roots and the soil. Thus, he says, “And behind it, a flame blazes.” He explains that before its arrival, the land was like the Garden of Eden, filled with every good thing, but behind it, it is like a wilderness. It is even worse than fire, for something can escape a fire, and people can rescue and save certain things from it; but from it there was no escape, for nothing at all was saved.
text.1_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Like the appearance: He portrays them as horses coming in wartime to conquer the land. A horse itself possesses the strength to charge forward with thunder and tumult; therefore, he says, “Their appearance is like the appearance of horses,” for they likewise advance with thunder and tumult. When a person rides the horse, so that he is called a horseman, it runs even faster because the rider drives it onward. Accordingly, he says, “And like horsemen, so they run,” for they too have a force compelling them to advance—the command and decree of Hashem riding upon them. When several horses are harnessed to a chariot, they pull it forward and produce the clattering sound of its wheels. Concerning this, he says:
text.1_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Like the sound of chariots, they leap upon the mountaintops: By joining together as one, they produce a noise like the sound of chariots. Although chariots do not ordinarily ascend mountaintops, they leap there with the sound of chariots.
text.1_Chapter, 4_Verse, 1_Comment: Like the sound: After depicting the locust swarm itself, he now depicts the sound produced by its activity as it destroys everything: it makes a noise like the sound of a flame of fire devouring stubble. Since he has already compared it to fire, he now says that its sound resembles the sound of a fiery flame as it consumes stubble. He then portrays how the locusts prepare themselves to descend from the mountains upon the cities, likening them to an army preparing for battle against the people who would obstruct their advance: they are like a mighty people prepared to wage war.
text.1_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: Before it: The peoples, however, tremble before it and do not dare to fight against it, while every face loses its radiance and splendor because of the overwhelming fear and anguish.
text.1_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Like mighty warriors: He now portrays how they conquer the city wall. First, they run toward the wall like mighty warriors, for the people defend themselves from the wall and at the gateway, so the attackers must charge courageously toward the wall and drive away its defenders. They must then know the tactics of warfare required to scale it. Therefore, he says, “Like men of war, they scale the wall.” The soldiers then assign a distinct route to each division, while also preserving a side path onto which it can turn if it must move sideways or encircle the enemy. This is called an “path.” Therefore, he says, “Each one proceeds on his own way,” referring to the main route, and “they do not deviate from their paths,” referring to the side paths.
text.1_Chapter, 7_Verse, 0_Comment: Nor does one press against another: They must also take care not to advance in disorder, lest one press against another and cause him to fall. Rather, each warrior proceeds along his own highway: each follows the route opened before him, neither too far from his companions nor crowded against them. Likewise, after scaling the wall and casting themselves down from it into the city, although swords and other weapons are held beneath them, they fall upon the weapons but are not wounded and suffer no harm.
text.1_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: In the city: He now depicts them after they have entered the city. There they rush about, making a noise in its streets; they run along the walls surrounding the houses and climb into the houses, entering not through the doorways but through the windows.
text.1_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Before it the earth trembles, and the heavens quake: This means that the established celestial order will be suspended, for the event will occur through the direct Providence of Hashem. In Isaiah 13:13, it says, “Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will quake from its place.” There, it means that Hashem would arrange and alter the celestial order so that Babylon would be destroyed through it. Here, however, it means that the event will not occur through the celestial order at all, but through Hashem alone. First, the earth trembles before Him, and consequently the heavens quake, for their governance is suspended by Hashem’s providential governance. Likewise, the sun and the moon grow dark, because their influence and governance are suspended, while the stars withdraw their radiance, for they no longer exert any influence or illumination.
text.1_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: And Hashem: He explains why the established celestial order will be suspended: because Hashem has raised His voice, commanding the event through His Providence. The meaning is that Hashem has raised His voice before His army: before the arrival of His army, He proclaimed and announced that although His camp is exceedingly vast—the locust swarm He sent to devastate the land—nevertheless, mighty is the one who fulfills His word. Whoever fulfills His command by repenting and abandoning his sins is mightier than His army and will overcome the locusts and drive them from the land. He further raised His voice to proclaim: “For the day of Hashem is great and exceedingly awesome,” referring to the day He appointed for punishing sinners; “and who can endure it?” That is, who will muster the strength to repent and thereby endure it—being able to withstand the day and bear its calamity without suffering harm? Hashem raised this voice before His army, meaning that many days before sending the army, He spoke through the prophet, who foretold all this in chapter 1. Nevertheless:
text.1_Chapter, 11_Verse, 0_Comment: Even now: Although the army has already arrived and the great day has already come, do not think that there is no remedy, for “even now, declares Hashem, return unto Me with all your heart.” He says, “return unto Me” even though I am now distant from you—as explained concerning the distinction between “return to Me” and “return unto Me” in Hosea 14:2. Your repentance must be with all your heart, not with a divided heart, and accompanied by fasting, weeping, and lamentation, representing confession and abandonment of sin.
text.1_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: And rend: Afterward, rend your hearts a second time—this signifies complete remorse for the past. Do not rend your garments over the calamity that has befallen you; rather, rend your hearts over your sins, for the sins you committed are more harmful to you than the calamity that befell you because of them. Return to Hashem: this is the second stage of repentance. After you have drawn near to Hashem, return to Him once more out of love. Then, because He is gracious and merciful and relents from evil, He will relent even now, although the locusts have already arrived and the calamity has begun.
text.1_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Whoever understands: He adds that even if the community as a whole is unwilling to repent, he nevertheless commands the individuals among them: whoever knows and understands should return and repent of his sins. Although an individual’s repentance will not suffice to annul the decree in its entirety, nevertheless, He may leave a blessing behind Him, so that a meal offering and a libation may remain for Hashem your God. He depicts the calamity as increasing in proportion to the number of sinners and sins. If one of them repents, the portion of the punishment corresponding to that person’s share in the collective evil will be diminished, leaving a meal offering and a libation for the House of Hashem.
text.1_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: Sound the shofar: (He now begins a third subject.) Until this point, he has spoken of the time when the locust swarm was approaching and advised the people to repent and annul the decree so that it would not come. He now speaks of the time when the locusts had already devastated the land, informing them that even then there remained a remedy by which they could be removed from the land. Therefore, he commands them to sound the shofar in Zion in order to assemble the people. He does not command them to sound an alarm blast to arouse fear, for they will already be frightened of their own accord now that the calamity has arrived.
text.1_Chapter, 14_Verse, 1_Comment: Sanctify a fast: Initially, he commanded the priests to sanctify the fast and proclaim a solemn assembly. Now he says that the people should arouse themselves to sanctify a fast, since the calamity has already arrived.
text.1_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: Gather the people: At first, he said, “Gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land,” meaning that they should assemble the elders, who would address them with words of admonition and thereby arouse the inhabitants of the land to repentance. Now that the calamity has actually arrived, the people should gather of their own accord, and the assembled congregation should sanctify themselves on their own. The people should gather the elders so that the elders may pray on their behalf, for it is no longer necessary for the elders to arouse and assemble the people. He commands them also to gather the young children and nursing infants, and to bring the bridegroom from his chamber, in order to increase the fasting and supplication.
text.1_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: Between the vestibule and the altar: Since he initially said that the priests should assemble the people, whereas here he states that the people should gather of their own accord, as explained above, without mentioning what the priests should do, he says that they should stand between the vestibule and the altar, weeping and praying. In their prayer they should say, “Spare Your people, O Hashem.” That is: 1) have compassion on them because they are Your people and You are their King; and 2) have compassion because the land is Your inheritance. The term “inheritance” indicates the sanctity within it and that Your Divine Presence rests upon it because of its holiness; therefore, do not subject it to disgrace. Because they are Your people, do not permit the nations to rule over them, for You are their King and Ruler. Because the land is Your inheritance, do not subject it to disgrace, lest the peoples say, “Where is their God?” This would disgrace the land as Your inheritance, where Your Divine Presence dwells and where You are their God.
text.1_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: And He became zealous: Hashem will hear their prayer. Corresponding to their plea, “Do not subject Your inheritance to disgrace,” which asks Him to defend the honor of the land that is His inheritance, “Hashem became zealous for His land”—that is, for the honor of His land. Corresponding to their plea, “Spare Your people, O Hashem,” it says, “and He had compassion on His people.” Our Sages said in the Midrash on Ruth: One verse states, “For Hashem will not forsake His people, for the sake of His great Name,” while another states, “For Hashem will not forsake His people.” When Israel fulfills the will of the Omnipresent, He acts for the sake of His people and His inheritance; when they do not fulfill His will, He acts for the sake of His great Name. The priests prayed that He would act for the sake of His great Name even though Israel was undeserving, as they said, “Why should the nations say, ‘Where is their God?’” Therefore, they said, “Spare Your people, O Hashem,” for there is a distinction between sparing and having compassion. One spares something because he needs it and refrains from destroying it for his own benefit—in this case, for the honor of Hashem’s Name, which is associated with Israel. Once Israel repented, however, He would act for the sake of His people and His inheritance, and Hashem would become zealous for His land. Therefore, it says, “and He had compassion on His people.” “Having compassion” means refraining from destroying something because of the worthiness of the thing itself, rather than because one needs it. Hashem would have compassion on them because of their own worthiness, now that they had become righteous. There are seven distinctions resulting from this. The first is that if He had acted solely for the sake of His great Name, He would have answered the priests, since they were the ones who prayed that He act for the honor of His Name. But since the deliverance came for the sake of His people and His inheritance, through Israel’s merit—
text.1_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: “Hashem answered and said to His people”: His answer would be addressed directly to the people themselves, in their own merit. If He had acted for the sake of His great Name while they themselves were undeserving, it should have said, “Behold, I am giving you the grain,” since it would not be theirs by virtue of their deeds but merely a gift from Him. Since He would act for their sake, however, it says, “Behold, I am sending you the grain,” for it belongs to them by virtue of their deeds. Its arrival had merely been delayed, and Hashem would send it to them because it was rightfully theirs and they deserved it through their merit. Furthermore, if He had acted only for the sake of His great Name, He would not have performed a miracle for them beyond the natural order. He would have given them only grain, which grows naturally when sown, but not new wine and oil, since the trees had already been destroyed, as explained in chapter 1, and could not naturally produce fruit. He therefore promises to perform a miracle for them in their merit, so that the new wine and the oil would also flourish. Moreover, if He had acted only for the sake of His great Name, so that it would not be profaned, He would have provided for them only sparingly—the minimum necessary to prevent the profanation of His Name. But since He would act in their merit, He says, “and you shall be satisfied with it”: He would give them an abundance sufficient to satisfy them. Finally, if He had acted only for the sake of His great Name, He would not have been concerned for the honor of an undeserving people, but only for the honor of His Name. Since He will act in their merit, however, He will safeguard their honor: “and I will no longer make you a disgrace among the nations.”
text.1_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: And the northern one: Furthermore, if the deliverance had been granted only for the sake of His Name, He would not have driven the locust swarm far away, so that it would remain nearby and ready to return should they continue to sin. But now, “I will remove it far from you”—the locust swarm that came from the north. Finally, if He had acted for the sake of His Name, He would have sent the swarm against the nations to avenge the honor of His Name, which they had scorned, and so that Israel would learn a lesson, as it says, “I have cut off nations … I said: Surely you will fear Me; you will accept correction.” Here, however, since I have acted for your sake, “I will drive it into a parched and desolate land.” Its vanguard: He depicts the swarm as having spread across the entire land, from sea to sea, moving from west to east. When the decree ended, it divided into two parts. The part standing in the east, which he calls “its vanguard,” would be carried into the eastern sea, while “its rear guard” would be carried into the western sea. “Its stench will rise”: when a locust swarm departs, it ordinarily leaves foulness and stench behind—foulness from the eggs it deposits and stench from the many locusts that die. The land consequently becomes putrid, causing pestilence and disease through the corruption of the air. He promises that this foulness and stench will rise and disappear, “for it has done great things.” This means that the swarm has already completed its mission and caused immense devastation. It also means that it has already accomplished much by bringing the people to repentance, so there is no need for it to inflict any further suffering. Our Sages interpreted this passage as referring to the evil inclination. Their meaning is that it is not the serpent that kills, but sin that kills: the evil inclination caused the locust swarm to come. When “the northern one”—the evil inclination concealed within the heart and inciting a person to sin—is driven away, its consequence, the locust swarm that came because of sin, will also be driven away.
text.1_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: Fear not, O ground: The word “ground” also denotes land that is not used as a grain field but as a place where trees grow, as explained above in 1:10. He explains that if the deliverance had been granted for the sake of His great Name alone, the trees would not have been restored, as explained above in verse 19. Since the deliverance came in your merit, however, even the ground where the trees grow will miraculously yield its produce in the form of fruit. Therefore, “rejoice and be glad,” for “rejoicing” denotes happiness over the appearance of something good that one had never imagined possible. Concerning this, he says, “for Hashem has done great things,” because the renewed growth of trees that had been destroyed is an extraordinary event beyond the natural order. Since Hashem has done this great thing miraculously, fear not, O ground.
text.1_Chapter, 21_Verse, 0_Comment: Fear not, O beasts of the field: If the deliverance had been granted only for the sake of His great Name, He would have restored the vegetation only in inhabited areas, not in the wilderness. But now, since it was granted for Israel’s sake, the pastures of the wilderness have also become green, and the tree has borne its fruit, although this occurred miraculously, as explained above. The deliverance thus encompassed every place and every kind of produce.
text.1_Chapter, 22_Verse, 0_Comment: And you, children of Zion: You, however, should not rejoice merely over temporal prosperity. Rather, rejoice and be glad in Hashem your God because Hashem has once again become favorably disposed toward you after you repented before Him. This should be the principal cause of your joy. You should therefore ultimately rejoice even over His having sent the locust swarm and famine upon you, for through them He compelled you to repent. Thus, rejoice because He has given you the teacher for righteousness: the locust swarm was the teacher that taught you to act righteously by observing the commandments between man and the Omnipresent. Ultimately, you will rejoice that He brought suffering upon you, for through it He taught you to improve your conduct. Because you learned righteousness and corrected your deeds, He will bring down rain for you—the early rain and the latter rain—in the first month, and the famine will depart from you. The law is that if the month of Kislev arrives without rainfall, the people fast twice in cycles of Monday, Thursday, and Monday, followed by seven additional fasts. If rain still does not fall, the community no longer fasts, since rainfall would then be of limited benefit, although individuals continue fasting until Nisan. If the season of Nisan begins and rain then falls, it is ordinarily a sign of a curse. Concerning this, he says, “Children of Zion, rejoice and be glad”: they had fasted until Nisan, and the rain came in Nisan—the early rain benefiting the trees and the latter rain benefiting the grain, since the trees’ season begins shortly before Passover, as stated in Tractate Taanit. Nevertheless, although the regular rainy season had already passed, this rain brought blessing, for:
text.1_Chapter, 23_Verse, 0_Comment: The threshing floors were filled with grain, and so forth, through Hashem’s miraculous blessing beyond the natural order.
text.1_Chapter, 24_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will repay you for the years: This may be compared to a mortal king who wages war against a province and is defeated by its inhabitants; he must then compensate them for the losses caused by his armies during the siege. Likewise, once you prevail through repentance performed out of love, I must repay you for what My armies destroyed when they consumed the produce of the land. Initially, he listed the cutting locust first, as it says, “What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust devoured.” Here, however, he lists the cutting locust last. When He first brought the cutting locust against them, it came as a just punishment for their evil deeds. Only afterward, when they began to repent, did the obligation to repay arise. He therefore did not need to repay them for what the cutting locust consumed at the beginning of its invasion, but only for what the swarming locust, the hopping locust, and the destroying locust consumed after they had already repented. He would likewise repay them for what the cutting locust consumed at the end, after they had repented. During that later period, the cutting locust operated together with the other species, and He must therefore repay them for the losses they caused.
text.1_Chapter, 25_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall eat abundantly and be satisfied: Beyond repaying them by increasing the produce until it makes up for what was lost during the years of famine, He will place a blessing within their bodies, so that they will eat a little and it will become blessed within them. This is the meaning of “you shall eat and be satisfied.” This blessing is a supernatural miracle and wonder. Therefore, “you shall praise the Name of Hashem your God,” who has directed His particular Providence toward you and “has dealt wondrously with you.” Through this, the glory of His great Name will be magnified. “And My people shall never be ashamed”: Earlier, He said, “I will no longer make you a disgrace among the nations.” There is a distinction between disgrace and shame: disgrace is inflicted by others, whereas shame is what one feels within oneself. This means that they will no longer be ashamed of their evil deeds, for through repentance out of love, their sins will be transformed into merits. He also alludes to the law explained in the Laws of Fasts: if the people have begun fasting and rain falls, they do not complete the fast. They first eat and afterward recite Hallel, for Hallel can be recited only from a state of satisfaction. This applies when their prayers are answered in the middle of the fast. He thus depicts Hashem answering them during their fast, whereupon they eat to satisfaction so that they may praise Him through the recitation of Hallel, which is recited only after one has eaten.
text.1_Chapter, 26_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall know: At first he said, “You shall praise the Name of Hashem.” The “Name” signifies how He is known and proclaimed from afar, for in the present age they do not know Hashem Himself—that is, the Divine Presence does not dwell permanently among them through continual miracles. They therefore praise only His Name, which is known to all through His general Providence. But in the future a day will come when you will know Him with absolute clarity, like one who apprehends something directly through the senses.
text.1_Chapter, 26_Verse, 1_Comment: For I am in the midst of Israel: I will continually remain among them and walk in their midst. I will not govern them through the agency of nature; rather, I am Hashem your God, and there is none besides Me. Nature and the celestial order will possess no power, for everything will be governed miraculously, without any intermediary. Then “My people shall never be ashamed.” At first, he said that they would not be ashamed of their evil deeds; now he adds that they will not suffer shame because of the absence of the Divine Presence and those things that were lacking in the Second Temple, which indicated that the Divine Presence did not dwell permanently among them as it had in earlier days. Then they will no longer be ashamed in this respect either, for they will be restored to their former state. This will occur at the End of Days, when the time of the future redemption arrives, as he will explain in the following chapters.
text.2_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall come to pass afterward: This refers back to his statement that a time will come when they will know Hashem with clear knowledge, because Hashem will be in their midst and His Divine Presence will dwell among them continually. This will occur at the End of Days, and he now prophesies concerning what will happen at that time. Abarbanel deduced from this that the preceding prophecy also concerns the four kingdoms, and that the four species of locusts are a parable and poetic image of four different kingdoms that will devour Israel completely. This is why the locusts are compared to a numerous people and a mighty nation, to horses, horsemen, chariots, and armed forces that wage war and conquer—all of which fits the subject represented by the parable. The plain meaning of the entire prophecy, however, does not support his interpretation, unless we say that while the prophet was prophesying about the locust swarm that actually appeared in those days, his spirit perceived a second, parallel prophecy concerning the four kingdoms, which resemble the swarm in also being four in number. According to what I have explained, however, there is no difficulty in the placement of this prophecy, for it follows directly from the statement, “And you shall know that I am in the midst of Israel,” which is itself a prophecy concerning the future. He therefore says that at the End of Days, when knowledge of Hashem increases below, an awakening from above will also arise, and He will pour out His Spirit upon them. “I will pour out My Spirit upon all flesh”: The Spirit of Hashem encompasses every spiritual faculty, as it says, “The Spirit of Hashem shall rest upon him: a spirit of wisdom and understanding, a spirit of counsel and strength, a spirit of knowledge and fear of Hashem.” Every spiritual influence bestowed upon a person by Hashem is called the Spirit of Hashem—whether it affects the body’s power through strength; the imaginative faculty through counsel and true intuition; the intellect through wisdom and understanding; or, above the intellect, the prophetic faculty through a spirit of knowledge and fear of Hashem. At that time He will pour out His Spirit upon all flesh in immense abundance, like water that spreads everywhere and covers everything equally. Nevertheless, distinctions will remain according to the preparedness of those who receive it. Thus, “your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.” There are three levels: complete prophecy; vision, which is below prophecy and consists of beholding visions while awake when the spiritual influence rests upon the imaginative faculty; and a true dream, which is below vision and contains a greater admixture of chaff and impurities, as it says, “The prophet who has a dream, let him relate the dream … What has the chaff to do with the grain?” (Jeremiah 23:28). The young sons and daughters, who will have been born in the generation of the Messiah and will therefore be prepared to receive the Divine Spirit, will experience complete prophecy. The elders, who were born in an earlier generation remote from the generation of the Messiah, will receive only true dreams, which are below vision and certainly below prophecy. The young men, who were likewise born before the Messiah’s arrival but closer to his time than the elders, will see visions, an intermediate level of spiritual influence between prophecy and dreams.
text.2_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And even upon the male and female servants: Upon those who live in those days, I will pour out My Spirit. Although they will not attain true dreams, much less the levels above them, a spirit of counsel, strength, fear of Hashem, and similar spiritual virtues will rest upon them.
text.2_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will display wonders: After explaining that knowledge of Hashem will then be revealed upon the earth through prophecy and Divine Inspiration, he says that they will also recognize Hashem through the appearance of signs and wonders that transcend the natural order. These wonders will encompass both the heavens and the earth. This will occur in two ways. First, through the punishment of the wicked, there will be blood, fire, and pillars of smoke. The wonder upon the earth will be blood—the slaughter that will occur among the armies of Gog and Magog, as described in Ezekiel. The wonder in the heavens will be fire, for He will rain fire, sulfur, and hailstones upon them, causing smoke to rise from the immense conflagration, until:
text.2_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: The sun will be transformed into darkness: The sun is the source of light, but it will then be transformed into darkness because of the fire and smoke produced by its burning heat, as it says, “Behold, the day is coming, burning like an oven.” The moon, which governs moisture, will be transformed into blood instead of water. That is, the celestial order will change to portend slaughter, conflagration, and destruction. All this will occur before the coming of the great day of Hashem, which is the great Day of Judgment.
text.2_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall come to pass: The second wonder will be the deliverance of the righteous: everyone who calls upon the Name of Hashem will escape, and the calamity will have no power over him. This will occur in two ways. On Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be deliverance, for everyone there will be saved, as it says, “He who remains in Zion … everyone inscribed for life in Jerusalem.” In other places, where not everyone will be saved, there will be deliverance among the survivors whom Hashem calls—that is, the righteous, everyone who calls upon Hashem and prays to Him.
text.3_Chapter, 0_Verse, 0_Comment: For behold: He explains when the events just mentioned will occur: when it is My intention to restore the captivity of Judah, meaning at the End of Days. Although the Ten Tribes will also be redeemed then, the tribe of Judah is foremost in His eyes.
text.3_Chapter, 1_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will gather all the nations: At that time, Hashem will cause all the nations to assemble for the war of Gog and Magog prophesied by Ezekiel. It is explained there that the descendants of Edom will first rise to wage war against the descendants of Ishmael, after which the descendants of Ishmael will fight against the descendants of Edom. This will be brought about by Hashem, to bring them down to the Valley of Jehoshaphat. He thus calls the Valley of Gog’s Multitude, where they will fall among the slain, “the Valley of Jehoshaphat.” He explains why it is given this name: “And I will enter into judgment with them there,” for there I will bring them to judgment concerning My people and My inheritance, Israel, because of the evils they committed against them. Although Hashem decreed exile upon Israel, the nations assisted in inflicting evil and exceeded the proper measure in two ways. First, “they scattered them among the nations”: because of the many expulsions and persecutions, Israel found no rest even in the lands of its enemies and was dispersed to every corner of the earth. Second, the nations took possession of Israel as though the people belonged to them and were property purchased with their money. This was expressed in “they divided My land,” as though they had acquired the land as an inheritance because they regarded Israel as their servants, and whatever a servant acquires belongs to his master.
text.3_Chapter, 2_Verse, 0_Comment: And for: They also took possession of their very bodies as purchased property and cast lots over them to determine who would take each one as a male or female servant. Israel was held in such contempt that they exchanged a boy for a prostitute: if an Israelite family had a son and a daughter, they gave the boy as payment to a prostitute and sold the girl for wine.
text.3_Chapter, 3_Verse, 0_Comment: Moreover: The nations into whose hands I delivered Israel, such as Assyria and Babylon, merely exceeded the proper measure, while the underlying harm they inflicted was ordained by Hashem. But what are you to Me, Tyre, Sidon, and all the regions of Philistia? I never delivered Israel into your hands at all; who commanded you to harm them? Are you repaying Me for something? Did I do you some harm for which you are now repaying Me evil for evil? What wrong have I done to you? There is a distinction between “recompensing” evil and “repaying” evil. One who repays evil has suffered harm from another because of that person’s hostility and hatred, and therefore repays him in kind—evil for evil. Recompensing evil, however, can apply even when one has suffered no harm from the other but harms him merely because of one’s own hostility toward him. Therefore, he says, “And if you are recompensing Me,” meaning: since I did you no harm for which you might repay Me evil for evil, you are acting solely because of your hostility toward Israel, even though Israel did you no harm. “Swiftly and speedily I will return your recompense upon your own heads.” I will therefore not wait until the final era and the future Day of Judgment, as I will with the other nations, but will swiftly repay you even in the present age. Indeed, in the days of Alexander the Great, Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia were destroyed and reduced to everlasting heaps of desolation.
text.3_Chapter, 4_Verse, 0_Comment: Because: He explains the evils they committed against Israel. Apart from the fact that “you took My silver and My gold”—for I did not deliver Israel’s possessions into your hands as I delivered them to Nebuchadnezzar, but you seized them on your own initiative—you committed still further wickedness, for:
text.3_Chapter, 5_Verse, 0_Comment: You sold the children of Judah to the Greeks at the time of the destruction, in order to remove them far from their own territory. This was worse than taking their silver for your own benefit or selling them as servants to profit from their price, for you sold them to a distant land out of sheer hostility and hatred. I will therefore return your recompense upon you in precisely the same manner in which you treated Israel—for this is the meaning of “returning”: bringing the very same thing back upon the one who did it.
text.3_Chapter, 6_Verse, 0_Comment: Behold, I will rouse them from the place: When the Greeks came and destroyed Tyre and Sidon, they brought their sons and daughters to Greece. There, the Jews who had been exiled to Greece purchased them from the Greeks and sold them to the Sabeans, a distant nation, thereby likewise removing them far from their own territory. Thus, they were punished through the very Jews whom they had sold and in precisely the same manner in which they had mistreated them.
text.3_Chapter, 8_Verse, 0_Comment: Proclaim: He now returns to the earlier subject, where he said that He would gather the nations in the Valley of Jehoshaphat. He commands that this be proclaimed among the nations by the decree of the heavenly Watchers and that they prepare for war. I have already explained in Ezekiel, chapters 32, 38, and 39, that in the future the nations of Edom will arise to conquer the land and will inflict great slaughter upon the Egyptians, who belong to the Ishmaelite faith. The Ishmaelites will then arise to avenge their brethren against the Edomites and will inflict great slaughter and destruction upon them. The Edomites will subsequently return to wage war against the descendants of Ishmael and will slaughter them. Thus, the war of Gog and Magog at the End of Days will occur in three stages. Concerning the first battle, he says, “Rouse the mighty warriors; let all the men of war approach and advance.” In this first battle, the mighty and those skilled in the tactics of warfare will be the combatants. In the second battle, there will no longer be mighty warriors or trained soldiers, for they will all have fallen among the slain. Then:
text.3_Chapter, 9_Verse, 0_Comment: Beat your plowshares into swords: Since all those who wielded swords will have fallen, the farmers and tillers of the soil will go in their place, fashioning new swords and spears from their plowshares and pruning hooks. They will not be mighty warriors; rather, the weak will say, “I am mighty.” In the third battle, after these too have perished in warfare, then:
text.3_Chapter, 10_Verse, 0_Comment: Hasten and come, all the surrounding nations: The remaining nations and multitudes will all go forth to fight a third time—Edom against Ishmael—without any military strength whatsoever, for there, O Hashem, You have brought down Your mighty warriors, and no mighty warrior will remain anywhere.
text.3_Chapter, 12_Verse, 0_Comment: Send forth: He again explains the three battles mentioned above. In the first, they are compared to grain still standing in the field and not yet harvested, for until then they had all lived peacefully in their own lands. He therefore commands the reapers to send forth the sickle, for the harvest is ripe and the time has come to reap it—that is, the full measure of their sins has been reached. In the second battle, he compares them to grapes that have already been gathered and placed in the winepress but have not yet been trodden to extract their wine. He therefore commands those who tread the grapes, “Come, descend,” into the winepress and tread them, “for the winepress is full,” and the time for treading has arrived. In the third battle, he compares them to grapes that have already been trodden, but whose wine has not yet been drawn off and separated from the seeds and skins. He therefore commands, “Let the vats overflow,” so that the wine will flow into the vat that receives the wine pressed from the grapes. He then explains the meaning of the parable: “for their wickedness is great.” They must therefore be trodden and trampled, as it says, “I have trodden the winepress alone … and I trod them in My anger.”
text.3_Chapter, 13_Verse, 0_Comment: Multitudes, multitudes: The reason vast multitudes will gather in the Valley of Jehoshaphat is that they will be in the Valley of Decision. It is called the “Valley of Jehoshaphat” at the time of judgment, when their case is examined and judgment is rendered to determine whether they are innocent or guilty. At that time, however, it will be called the Valley of Decision, because the judgment will already have been decided and concluded: they are condemned to destruction. Therefore, the day of Hashem is near, and He will hasten to destroy them in the Valley of Decision, since their judgment has already been decided and finalized.
text.3_Chapter, 14_Verse, 0_Comment: The sun and the moon grow dark: This means that the influences of the heavenly bodies will then be suspended, and the stars will withdraw their radiance and cease to exert influence through the celestial order.
text.3_Chapter, 15_Verse, 0_Comment: And Hashem will roar from Zion: From there Divine governance and judgment will issue. A roar denotes a mighty sound, the opposite of a low voice, whereas “raising His voice” does not necessarily indicate a loud sound, but merely that He will not remain silent and will make His voice heard. In Zion, the principal dwelling place of His Divine Presence, He will roar with a mighty voice until it becomes known to everyone. From Jerusalem, which does not possess the same degree of sanctity as Zion, He will not roar so loudly, but neither will He remain silent; rather, He will raise His voice, signifying Divine governance. Through this roar, the heavens and the earth will quake, and both the natural order governing the earth and the celestial order governing the heavens will be suspended. But Hashem will be a refuge for His people and a stronghold for the children of Israel. Because they are His people, He will be their refuge, protecting them from every evil so that it does not befall them. Because they are the children of Israel—a name indicating that they transcend the natural order, as it says, “For you have striven with Divine beings”—He will be their stronghold, enabling them to prevail through the might of Hashem, which is greater than mere refuge.
text.3_Chapter, 16_Verse, 0_Comment: And you shall know: Then you will know with absolute clarity that I am Hashem your God. This is what was stated above: “You shall know that I am in the midst of Israel and that I am Hashem your God,” dwelling in Zion, My holy mountain. That is, “I am in the midst of Israel” because My Divine Presence dwells continually in Zion. Jerusalem will also be holy, and strangers will no longer pass through it. Zion, however, will possess an even greater degree of holiness, so that even Israelites will refrain from entering it unnecessarily.
text.3_Chapter, 17_Verse, 0_Comment: And it shall come to pass on that day: Divine abundance and blessing will increase exceedingly, until the mountains drip with sweet wine because of the abundance of sweet fruit, the hills flow with milk because of the multitude of cattle and sheep, and all the channels of Judah flow with water. Until then, there had been a shortage of water both throughout the Land of Israel generally and in Jerusalem particularly, since Jerusalem had no springs. At that time, not only will there be water in Judah, but a spring will also issue from the House of Hashem. A fountain will open there and spread outward until it waters the Valley of Shittim. According to Rabbi Saadia Gaon, this refers to the Jordan, which is near Shittim; according to Rashi, it means the Valley of Shittim literally. Ezekiel and Zechariah had already prophesied concerning this spring. Allegorically, the Torah and faith, which are compared to water, will flow from there to the entire world. Since Israel first broke out in sexual immorality and idolatry at Shittim through the worship of Baal Peor, and this was the beginning of Israel’s sin, he indicates that the holy spring will purify the defilement that began in the Valley of Shittim and remove corrupt beliefs and desires.
text.3_Chapter, 18_Verse, 0_Comment: Egypt: This includes the adherents of the faith of Ishmael. The chief destroyers of the First Temple were Assyria and Babylon, which later came under the faith represented by Egypt. From there the first war of Gog and Magog will begin, when the descendants of Edom rise against them and destroy them, as explained in Ezekiel’s prophecies. Then Egypt will become desolate. Afterward, the descendants of Ishmael will rise against the descendants of Edom, who destroyed the Second Temple through the Romans, the foremost of the nations of Edom. Concerning this, he says that Edom will become a desolate wilderness, as I explained in Ezekiel, chapters 32, 38, and 39. All this will occur because of the violence committed against the children of Judah during the two destructions.
text.3_Chapter, 19_Verse, 0_Comment: But Judah will be inhabited forever: Ephraim had formerly separated from Judah and Jerusalem, but at that time they will be reunited. Judah will never again go into exile, and Jerusalem will never again be destroyed, throughout all generations.
text.3_Chapter, 20_Verse, 0_Comment: And I will avenge their blood that I have not yet avenged: The war of Gog and Magog will include only the nations of Edom and Ishmael and those associated with their faiths. Yet there are many other peoples who do not belong to either group and who also shed Israel’s blood. He therefore says that afterward He will avenge the blood that He did not yet avenge through Gog’s defeat—that is, the blood shed by nations that did not participate in the war of Gog and Magog. This will occur after Hashem dwells in Zion, when He will avenge the remaining bloodshed and bring those nations to justice.
